description: We are a globally connected collective of curious, programming-minded individuals united by our passion for space exploration. Bringing together diverse perspectives from India, Bangladesh, and Nigeria, we have collaborated across geographical and cultural boundaries to bring this project to life. Driven by the ambition to contribute to the future of space exploration and work alongside NASA, we see this hackathon as an opportunity to learn, innovate, grow, and hopefully emerge victorious.
summary: Beyond the Known built a wildfire intelligence platform for the MODIS/VIIRS challenge. NASA FIRMS publishes hundreds of millions of satellite thermal anomalies, but raw detections are noisy and cannot be read as a threat picture. We ingest the full 2000–2026 record — 458,262,571 detections from MODIS Terra/Aqua and VIIRS (NOAA-20, NOAA-21, SNPP) — and apply cleaning rules for confidence, valid coordinates and duplicates, leaving 164,025,421. Those are then fused into events and fires by space-time clustering, collapsing the archive into 60,445,399 compact fire records stored as Parquet and served through DuckDB and FastAPI. A Leaflet interface lets anyone search a region, see clustered activity, and open any fire to read its duration, detection count, FRP totals, centroid, contributing sensors and event timeline. We validated the pipeline end to end on a real 24-hour FIRMS slice: 150,844 detections became 53,104 events and 30,430 fires. It matters because responders need one clear fire record, not a raw satellite feed.
details:
Project Details

Our project addresses the challenge of harmonizing active fire hotspot observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors. These sensors provide valuable information about fire activity, but differences in their spatial resolutions, detection characteristics, and observation patterns can create inconsistencies when their datasets are compared or analysed together.

How it works:
Our proposed system brings MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations into a unified data-processing workflow. It focuses on cleaning the incoming observations, identifying potential duplicate detections, organizing the datasets, and generating meaningful summaries for analysis. Rather than repeatedly processing enormous raw datasets, we explored a more efficient architecture using compressed Parquet files, DuckDB for in-memory analytical queries, and FastAPI for serving processed information. This approach is intended to reduce storage overhead and improve retrieval efficiency.

Benefits and intended impact:
The project aims to make multi-sensor hotspot information more consistent, accessible, and useful. Better harmonization can support wildfire monitoring, environmental research, temporal analysis, and disaster-management decisions. It also offers a foundation for exploring more reliable fire-detection patterns across different satellite platforms.

Tools and technologies:
Our technical exploration includes Python, Parquet, Zstandard compression, DuckDB, FastAPI, and JSON-based data delivery. The project is primarily software- and data-processing-oriented, without requiring specialized physical hardware.

Creativity and design considerations:
Our approach combines satellite-data harmonization with efficient data engineering. We considered dataset volume, storage efficiency, retrieval speed, duplicate observations, differences in sensor characteristics, and the preservation of meaningful hotspot information. Our goal is not simply to combine two datasets, but to make their observations more comparable and computationally practical for further analysis.
